I've redesigned the persona note card. It's now one slim bar of voice controls with the note's words directly below. I checked it in Storybook (single note, conversation and phone width), and type-check and lint pass on the touched files. I didn't run the e2e suite.

**What's gone:**
- **Name, role and label line ("on clarity").** The face and the card colour already tell you who it is.
- **The quoted passage.** The card opens right beside the marked text, so the quote was a second copy.
- **"Filed against 'The public room'".**
- **The repeated header on replies.** Each of the persona's replies used to carry a 56px face with name and role. Replies are now plain bubbles. A small face appears only if a different persona joins the thread.
- **"You" and "M. Le Stylo is typing…".** Your replies sit on the right; the persona's are in their colour on the left. "Typing" is now just three dots.
- **The "⌘↩ to reply" footer and separate Reply/Strike row.**

**What's prominent now:**
- **Talk** is a filled button in the persona's colour and the most visible thing on the card. Clicking the face also starts a voice conversation.
- **Listen** is a bordered button that changes to Pause/Resume while the note is read aloud.
- **Strike** is small text in the same bar, next to close.
- **Writing back** is the last option: a single "Or write back…" box at the bottom with its own mic for dictating a reply. It reuses the shared composer, so dictation works the same as elsewhere in the app. **Enter now sends; it used to be ⌘↩.**
- **The note text** is now 1rem with more room around it.

I also fixed a blank line that showed at the bottom of every reply bubble. Markdown already handles line breaks, so I removed the extra whitespace setting that caused it.

- `SpeakButton` has a new `labelled` option.
- `ChatComposer` can now pass `data-*` attributes to its text box, so unsent reply drafts are still saved.
- `twyne-editor.tsx` saves a dictated draft into the same place typed drafts go.

**Decision for you:** the card now shows two mic icons, Talk (live conversation) and the composer's mic (dictate a written reply). They have different tooltips but look alike. If that's confusing, I'd remove the composer's mic, so the card offers Talk for voice and the text box for typing.

agent 2026-10-28T08:28:29.633Z I think this works, but as a fallback path. It shouldn't replace Live. Here's what I found.

**Where Twyne already is.** Most of the plumbing exists:
- **Desktop app:** it already runs a local model server, `desktop/litert-server.ts`.
- **Local text models:** `evals/run-local-model.ts` already tests LFM2.5-2.6B as the local engine, served through llama.cpp's `llama-server --jinja`.
- **Voice parts:** speech output already runs in the browser (`src/utils/supertonic-tts.ts`). The Live voice desk is separate from the provider: the tools, edit proposals and apply/discard steps live in `live-voice-contract` and `live-voice-workspace`. A local voice model could reuse all of that.

**What I could confirm about LFM3** (the release is a day old, so coverage is thin):
- **Sizes and cost:** the audio model and Omni are about 2B parameters. The hosted API charges $2 per million audio-input tokens and $10 per million audio-output tokens. Liquid says the first response token can arrive about 50ms after speech ends, but that's their best case.
- **Running it locally:** llama.cpp can run the text side, and speech-to-text is still a pending pull request there. Full two-way voice chat currently needs Liquid's Python runtime. I found nothing on running it in the browser (WebGPU/ONNX), and only one third-party blog mentions full-duplex at all.
- **Vision:** you're right that Twyne doesn't need it. Omni would mean downloading vision weights for nothing, so the audio-only model is the better pick.
- **The decision model:** I couldn't confirm "D1" from the sources I found. Can you send me a link?

**How I'd build it:**
1. **Desktop first.** Run LFM3 audio as a local server next to `litert-server` and point the Live relay at it with the same event shape. Live voice would then work offline and cost nothing on desktop.
2. **Web next.** The web version can't run the Python runtime, so voice there has to stay hosted until a WebGPU/ONNX build ships. One caveat on the out-of-credits fallback: it only works if the user has a local runtime (desktop, or a local server they set up).
3. **Use the decision model in place of Jev.** It would run the local `judgement` and `interpret` steps. That takes Jev's 503s and the per-action $0.25 holds out of the voice loop.
4. **Choose automatically.** Use hosted Live when there's enough credit and the gateway is healthy, otherwise use local, and let the user override it in settings.

Before building, I'd test it the way `run-local-model.ts` tests LFM2.

agent 2026-10-28T08:28:45.801Z For live conversation, yes, very likely. For read-aloud narration, I wouldn't assume it yet. A correction first: there's no Kokoro in the code. In-browser speech is Supertonic only (`src/utils/supertonic-tts.ts`); OpenAI and Fish voices go through providers.

**Where LFM3 audio should win:** Supertonic only turns text into speech. A local Live mode built on it would chain three separate models: speech-to-text, a text model, then Supertonic. You'd wait for each step in turn, and it can't handle being interrupted. LFM3 audio is one model that listens and speaks, so it can respond while you're still talking and handle interruptions. For Live it's a different kind of thing, not a small upgrade.

**Where Supertonic still holds up:**
- **Size:** Supertonic is about 260 MB (the files listed in `browser-inference.ts`) and already runs in the browser with WebGPU, falling back to WASM. LFM3 audio is about 2.2B parameters, roughly 1.5 GB or more even compressed, and I found no browser runtime for it yet.
- **Narration:** reading a chapter aloud doesn't need conversation, just good, consistent voices. Supertonic's fixed voice embeddings are made for exactly that. I haven't seen anything on LFM3's voice quality, its voice choices, or how it holds up over long passages.

**My suggestion:**

- Keep Supertonic for in-browser narration until a side-by-side test says otherwise. I can add that test to the LFM3 eval: the same passages through both, judged on clarity, pacing and voice consistency.

I've pushed v0.26.0 to main, and Railway is building it for production now. I'll confirm once that deploy finishes.

**What went out:**
- **Persona note card:** the compact two-box design with icon controls and compact warnings.
- **Faces on note anchors:** each anchor shows the persona's face, or your profile photo, in their colour. This came from the other thread, which couldn't take screenshots. When I checked it here, the face showed up as a tiny squeezed strip instead of a face. The editor's image styling was causing that, so I fixed it.
- **Your dropdown bug:** the "canonical uses left alone" disclosure in the Organization & Flow lens no longer closes when you hover its passages. I added a test that hovers the rows, and the 10 living desk tests pass, run twice.
- **Storybook stories and preview hooks** for the editor cards, inline review and the rubric panel, from the other thread.
- **Local Live voice over WebGPU,** from `t3/live-voice-local-webgpu`. It adds two packages, `onnxruntime-web` and `@huggingface/tokenizers`, which are now part of the production build. Its 32 tests pass, but I haven't tried offline voice in a browser.
- **Everything already on this branch since 0.25.0:** the account page, forecasts, research scoring, the sync fixes, and Main's one new merge.

**Checks before pushing:** full type-check is clean, the client and server builds succeed, and the 412 tests I ran pass. I didn't run the whole test suite.

**Release:** `package.json` is at 0.26.0 with an annotated `v0.26.0` tag, and `CHANGELOG.md` has a new 0.26.0 entry. Pushing the tag started the GitHub release build, and CI is running on main.
